title: How Virat Kohli Rewrote the T20 Playbook
subtitle: The Reinvention Hidden Inside the Numbers
description: The Reinvention Hidden Inside the Numbers
blocks: By the time most batters get to their mid-thirties, what we usually expect is they stop changing their method**.** Certainly, like every other batter, they do have their flaws but over all these years, we had created an image which speaks about a certain nature of Cricket we expect them to play till they retire. Virat Kohli though had a different idea; he evolved due to the brand of cricket Team India wanted to play after that Adelaide horror in 2022.

Between 2021 and 2024, Kohli was still one of the most feared batters in the IPL. Yes, he had faced a slight dip, but the sheer volume of runs he scores every season make him a dependable batter. His average of **40**, a strike rate of **130**, all of it was still formidable. But somewhere in the rapidly changing nature of the T20s, his method was becoming slightly negative towards his team.

As a batter in T20s, your goal should be to play in a way that maximizes the **Win%** of your team in all the phases. The issue with Virat was bowlers had quietly been working out his method: Virat Kohli at the start of an innings was very different from Virat Kohli once he’d settled in. He would leave the big shots until he had seen the bowler and found his rhythm.

His 1st 15 balls in every game was a crucial window for the bowlers, a window where bowlers wanted to bowl at **him** rather than the opposite batter, to minimise the runs lost in the Powerplay. (**Win Percentage Added = 2.29 %** per match IPL 2021-24 vs **3.56 %** in IPL 2025-26)

The strike rate in those first 15 balls of an innings in 2021-24: **130.3**, with a dot ball percentage of **42.8%**. Nearly one in two balls was a non-scoring delivery. For a player of his calibre, that was a number opposition tried to exploit.
By 2025-26, that same first-15-ball strike rate had become **156.2**, with dots down to **34%**. A 26-run improvement per hundred balls, from the moment the first delivery is bowled.
What changed? Everything. And it starts with one shot.
The Numbers Are Worth Sitting With First

Before the story, let’s establish the scale of the transformation which Virat completed. Overall, Kohli went from a strike rate of **129.84** and average of **40** in 2021-24 to a strike rate of **153** and average of **52** in 2025-26. Dot balls fell from **35.6%** to **30.0%**. He went from hitting a boundary every **6** balls to every **5** balls.

Those are meaningful improvements for any batter. But if we closely observe the background of the story, what was happening in his team RCB, and then what was the impact of Virat’s newfound method on the team’s performance, this looks even more important. The biggest takeaway is how Virat has helped them to win the Powerplay battle. **65%** of the IPL matches are decided in the Powerplay.

In the first six overs, Kohli’s strike rate went from **134.62 to 156.52**. His dot ball percentage in the Powerplay fell from **43.02% to 35.12%**. He went from hitting a boundary every 4.71 balls to every 3.83 balls.

This is like a completely different batter, because the stats do suggest that. But averages and strike rates are the result. The story is in what changed underneath them and that is one of the more fascinating reinventions I’ve seen a batter undertake at this stage of a career.
Chapter I: The Plan The Bowlers Had
Let’s go back to 2021-24. Cricket teams were slowly moving the analytical way now. (I think they’re still slow to this day...)
Against Kohli, the map showed something useful: *back it up short.*

The real plan was subtler. **Short** **of a good length**. That irritating back-of-a-length corridor that sits between the drive and the pull. Where you can’t really get under it, and you can’t really get on top of it either. Where you’re either pushing tentatively through mid-off, or cutting behind point, or steering to third man.

In 2021-24, when Kohli faced short-of-good-length deliveries from pace bowlers, he was doing exactly that. His response was scattered: **steered (14.2%)**, **cut (12.5%)**, **flicked (12.5%)**, **cover drove (8.2%)**. The pull — the response that actually punishes this length appeared in just **14.9%** of those balls.
The overall strike rate on short-of-good-length pace deliveries: **119.9**. The pacers had known where to ball and they used to exploit it pretty well.
Somewhere between 2024, Virat Kohli started treating short-of-good-length pace as something to attack.

He was limited to third man and cover region against back of a length deliveries but now, that instead of steering those to third man he’s pulling them to square leg. He used to score **1.5%** less than the league average right hander but now scores nearly **4%** more than him in square leg region against short of a good length deliveries.

In 2025-26, the **pull shot** on short-of-good-length pace went from **14.9%** to **25.7%** of deliveries. The steer that bleeds singles and dots in roughly equal measure fell from **14.2% to 5.7%**. Cut shot increased from **12.5%** to **18.1%**.
Also, he’s pulling with significantly better control: Pull shot control vs pace rose from **61.5% to 68.1%**.
What This Did to Right-Arm Fast Bowlers in the Powerplay
This is where the story becomes remarkable as we understand how this contributed to RCB’s batting strength. RCB started to win more in the Powerplay phase due to Virat’s adaptation.
Against right-arm fast bowlers in the Powerplay between 2021 and 2023, Kohli scored at **144.4**. Already above the league average of 123.5. The RAA (Runs Above Average) was +27.8.

By 2024-26, that number became **176**. The league average in the same conditions moved from 123.5 to 144.3, a 21-point improvement. Kohli’s moved 32 points. His RAA against right-arm fast bowling in the Powerplay jumped from +27.8 to **+32.5**.
The wagon zones tell the story of how. In 2021-24, his primary scoring region against RF in the Powerplay was **Covers (22%).**
By 2025-26, covers had dropped to **15%**. But Square leg jumped from **9.6%** to **12.73%**. Mid wicker, Mid On jumped too.

This is what the pull shot transformation looks like on a wagon wheel. When you start pulling short-of-good-length deliveries with purpose and control, the scoring goes leg-side and square. You also start forcing bowlers to bowl fuller to avoid the pull and when they do, you can drive them all over the field from Cover to Mid on. What was once a back-of-a-length plan is now a back-of-a-length problem for the bowler.
The Domino Effect: Every Length Becomes a Threat

When bowlers can’t bowl back of a length to Kohli, they have to bowl full. And when they bowl full to Virat Kohli, they’re back on his turf. The cover drive, the on drive, the straight drive all were unleashed.
His strike rate against good-length deliveries outside off stump went from **116.3 to 138.0**, with the dot ball percentage falling from **39.8%** to **33.1%.**

The dismissals confirm the power shift. Against Right arm Fast bowlers in the Powerplay in 2021-24, he was dismissed 6 times in 133 balls. In 2025-26, just 2 times in 86 balls. And both of those dismissals — one pull caught at mid-on, one steered catch behind were uncontrolled rather than technical failures.
Chapter III: The First Fifteen, No Longer A Window

In 2021-24, Kohli’s first 15 balls of an innings produced a strike rate of **130.3** with a dot ball percentage of **42.8%.** After ball 15, his strike rate was **129.4** which is almost identical. He was batting at roughly the same pace throughout, having spent the first phase settling in. He couldn’t go after it from ball one.

In 2025-26, the first 15 balls produce a strike rate of **156.2** with dots at **34.0%**. After ball 15, it’s **136.6,** actually lower. But he attacks from ball one now. The pull shot weaponization is part of why: if the fast bowlers come at you in the Powerplay with back-of-a-length plans, you are now equipped to punish them immediately, from the very first delivery. And the SR after the Powerplay isn’t an issue but a necessity, Virat’s attacking job is done after the Powerplay because Virat playing attacking shots in the middle overs, taking risk, isn’t the best solution for RCB, rather it’s the role for the likes of **Padikkal**, **Patidar, Krunal and Jitesh**. T20 is a role-playing game. Virat plays the second fiddle and that is important for RCB to win more.
Chapter IV: The Middle Overs Puzzle

Against spin bowlers in middle overs between 2021 and 2023, Virat Kohli was scoring at a strike rate of **100.0.** The league average in that same phase was **123.4**. He was **23.4 points below the average IPL batter** against spin in the middle overs. He was scoring at a pace that, against the background of how modern T20 batting has evolved, was not ideal for any team he was batting in.
In 2021-23, against spin in the middle overs, Kohli was dismissed **8 times**. He was hitting a boundary every **14.2 balls**, which was poor.
What specifically troubled him more was Off spin, not many talk about this and yes it is surprising as he’s a Right hander, but Off breaks troubled him.

Against off-spinners in 2021-23, Kohli was scoring at SR of only **82.1**. The league average was **121.7**. He was sitting **39.5 points below the league average** against off-spin. Four dismissals in 56 balls and a dot % of **39.3%**.
In the middle overs specifically where off-spinners operate most effectively his SR was **79.1**. Against a league average of **118.7**. A difference of **-39.7 percentage points**.

These are ordinary numbers to have against any bowler type at this level. To have them against off-spin, a bowler variation that the right handed batters are usually expected to dominate, tells you everything about the nature of the plan.
The Pitch Maps Tell the Story
The pitchmaps against off-spin across the two eras are almost uncomfortably clear.
In 2021-23, the ball that got Kohli out repeatedly was a very specific delivery: **good length, outside off stump**.

By 2024-26: zero dismissals against off-spin. The bowlers are still bowling there but you can see the volume of deliveries have have shifted from outside off stump to on the stumps but they’re not getting him out anymore. Also, off spinners are bowling more fuller to him now, and this change is because Virat forced them to do so.
Chapter V: The Slog Sweep - A Shot That Wasn’t There

For Rohit Sharma against left-arm spin, it was the sweep transformed from a minor part of his game to a weapon that accounted for **28%** of his runs against Slow Left Arm bowlers. Virat too did something similar.
Against all spin bowlers in 2021-23, the slog sweep contributed **4.1%** of Kohli’s runs with a Control rate of **50%**, which was of course low.

However, by 2024-26: the slog sweep contributes **17.2%** of all his runs against spin. That’s a **4x multiplication** in usage and run contribution from a single shot. That shot is why the off-spin plan stopped working.

When we close our eyes imagining Virat playing against off spinner, we can just naturally envision him driving the good length ball towards long off for a single. But now when you bowl there the slog sweep scores off those deliveries and forces the bowler to bowl more fuller, and when they do that they play into the hands of Kohli.

Between 2021-23 and 2024-26, Kohli’s runs in Mid wicket have doubled. His leg-side run percentage against spin in the middle overs (square leg plus mid-wicket combined) went from **37%** to **56%**. Against a league average that barely moved 29.0% to 29.3%, his leg-side dominance against spin went from **+6.3pp above league to +13.7pp above league**. The mid wicket which contributed 25.53% of his runs against off spin, now contributes 52.87% which is more than half.
The Bowler-Type Picture: The Only Plan Left

There is one area where Kohli is still below league average: Slow left arm bowlers. In 2021-23 his SR against them was 100.5, league was 123.5. In 2024-26, he’s at 122.3 against a league of 138.2. Below league in both eras, though the deficit narrowed from **-23pp** to **-15.9pp**.

The slow left-arm plan still holds some value. However, in RCB this changes. He’s playing with partners like Padikkal, Patidar and sometimes Krunal in the middle overs which either keeps the SLA out of the game or is taken down by his partner. This is a proper partnership.

He’s found the balance that T20 cricket at the highest level requires: don’t lose the wicket in the middle overs and let the Powerplay do the damage. Virat is winning the battles in the Powerplay with such dominance that the game has often already tilted by the time spinners get their extended runs.

He identified a specific, structural problem in how bowling attacks were setting him up. The back-of-a-length plan and the tentative start. He kind off thought about this from the opposition’s perspective. That realization was enough for him to adapt his batting which now significantly contributes in RCB’s winning machine. He saw how teams were setting up for him, and he changed before they could keep using the same plan. That is the point of the whole piece.
